claim: The majority (96.2%) of ribosome footprints was mapped onto the annotated coding sequences (CDS).
source: The majority (96.2%) of ribosome footprints was mapped onto the annotated coding sequences (CDS), and its distribution displayed a clear 3-nt periodicity, reflecting the codon-wise movement (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports a specific percentage of ribosome footprints mapped to CDS based on their sequencing data analysis.

claim: Ribosome footprint distribution displayed a clear 3-nt periodicity, reflecting the codon-wise movement.
source: The majority (96.2%) of ribosome footprints was mapped onto the annotated coding sequences (CDS), and its distribution displayed a clear 3-nt periodicity, reflecting the codon-wise movement (Figure 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed 3-nt periodicity in the data and references Figure 1B showing this pattern.

claim: The transcript level and the number of ribosome footprints did not always match, suggesting substantial posttranscriptional regulations (R2 = 0.664).
source: As previously reported, the transcript level and the number of ribosome footprints did not always match, suggesting substantial posttranscriptional regulations (R2 = 0.664; Figure 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation coefficient from their data analysis and cites previous reports.

claim: Shaker (Sh) and Trehalase (Treh) were similar regarding transcript levels.
source: For instance, while Shaker (Sh) and Trehalase (Treh), which encode a voltage-gated K+ channel and an enzyme that hydrolyzes trehalose, respectively, were similar regarding transcript levels, far more ribosome footprints were detected on Treh (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed similarity in transcript levels between these two genes from their RNA-seq data.

claim: Far more ribosome footprints were detected on Treh compared to Shaker.
source: For instance, while Shaker (Sh) and Trehalase (Treh), which encode a voltage-gated K+ channel and an enzyme that hydrolyzes trehalose, respectively, were similar regarding transcript levels, far more ribosome footprints were detected on Treh (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed differences in ribosome footprints from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Shaker encodes a voltage-gated K+ channel.
source: For instance, while Shaker (Sh) and Trehalase (Treh), which encode a voltage-gated K+ channel and an enzyme that hydrolyzes trehalose, respectively, were similar regarding transcript levels, far more ribosome footprints were detected on Treh (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Shaker gene.

claim: Trehalase encodes an enzyme that hydrolyzes trehalose.
source: For instance, while Shaker (Sh) and Trehalase (Treh), which encode a voltage-gated K+ channel and an enzyme that hydrolyzes trehalose, respectively, were similar regarding transcript levels, far more ribosome footprints were detected on Treh (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Trehalase gene.

claim: TE was much higher for Treh than Sh.
source: We therefore measured TE, ribosome footprints normalized by mRNA reads. TE was much higher for Treh than Sh (Figure 1F), and we found a striking genome-wide variability with more than 20-fold TE difference between the 5 and 95 percentiles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated TE values from their data.

claim: There is a striking genome-wide variability with more than 20-fold TE difference between the 5 and 95 percentiles.
source: We therefore measured TE, ribosome footprints normalized by mRNA reads. TE was much higher for Treh than Sh (Figure 1F), and we found a striking genome-wide variability with more than 20-fold TE difference between the 5 and 95 percentiles (Figure 1G).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated TE variability from their genome-wide data.

claim: Transcripts involved in fatty acid metabolism and proteasome are actively translated.
source: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genome (KEGG) pathway enrichment analysis revealed that the transcripts involved in fatty acid metabolism and proteasome are actively translated (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports results from KEGG pathway enrichment analysis of their data.

claim: Ribosome proteins are enriched in transcripts with low TE.
source: In contrast, ribosome proteins, as previously reported (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Cho et al., 2015), and proteins mediating neuronal ligand–receptor interactions were significantly enriched in the transcripts with low TE, suggesting translational suppression (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from their data analysis and cites previous reports.

claim: Proteins mediating neuronal ligand–receptor interactions were significantly enriched in the transcripts with low TE, suggesting translational suppression.
source: In contrast, ribosome proteins, as previously reported (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Cho et al., 2015), and proteins mediating neuronal ligand–receptor interactions were significantly enriched in the transcripts with low TE, suggesting translational suppression (Figure 1H).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from their data analysis and interprets them as suggesting translational suppression.

claim: Many transcripts encoding ligand- or voltage-gated ion channels, G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) showed remarkably low TE.
source: Indeed, many transcripts encoding ligand- or voltage-gated ion channels, G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR) showed remarkably low TE (Figure 1C and I).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed low TE values for these gene categories from their data.

claim: UAS-RpL3::FLAG on the third chromosome exhibited minimum leakage expression in the brain.
source: By immunohistochemistry, we confirmed that UAS-RpL3::FLAG on the third chromosome exhibited minimum leakage expression in the brain and did not display any apparent morphological defects upon expression using either driver compared to other insertions or constructs (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2012; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunohistochemistry results confirming minimal leakage expression.

claim: UAS-RpL3::FLAG did not display any apparent morphological defects upon expression using either driver.
source: By immunohistochemistry, we confirmed that UAS-RpL3::FLAG on the third chromosome exhibited minimum leakage expression in the brain and did not display any apparent morphological defects upon expression using either driver compared to other insertions or constructs (Chen and Dickman, 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Thomas et al., 2012; Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observations from immunohistochemistry comparing to other constructs.

claim: The exogenously expressed RpL3::FLAG was highly concentrated in cell bodies but also detectable in neurites.
source: The exogenously expressed RpL3::FLAG was highly concentrated in cell bodies but also detectable in neurites, consistent with the subcellular localization of the endogenous ribosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed subcellular localization from imaging data.

claim: The subcellular localization of exogenously expressed RpL3::FLAG is consistent with the subcellular localization of the endogenous ribosome.
source: The exogenously expressed RpL3::FLAG was highly concentrated in cell bodies but also detectable in neurites, consistent with the subcellular localization of the endogenous ribosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: The manuscript compares their observations to endogenous ribosome localization shown in their data.

claim: Footprints were found on 10,821 (78.4% of all the annotated genes) genes in neurons.
source: Through the purification of FLAG-tagged ribosomes, we successfully profiled translatome from neurons and glial cells in the fly heads: footprints were found on 10,821 (78.4% of all the annotated genes) and 10,994 (79.7%) genes in neurons and glia, respectively, with decent reproducibility among the biological replicates (R2 > 0.9, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of genes with footprints from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Footprints were found on 10,994 (79.7%) genes in glia.
source: Through the purification of FLAG-tagged ribosomes, we successfully profiled translatome from neurons and glial cells in the fly heads: footprints were found on 10,821 (78.4% of all the annotated genes) and 10,994 (79.7%) genes in neurons and glia, respectively, with decent reproducibility among the biological replicates (R2 > 0.9, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number and percentage of genes with footprints from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: The cell-type-specific Ribo-seq showed decent reproducibility among the biological replicates (R2 > 0.9).
source: Through the purification of FLAG-tagged ribosomes, we successfully profiled translatome from neurons and glial cells in the fly heads: footprints were found on 10,821 (78.4% of all the annotated genes) and 10,994 (79.7%) genes in neurons and glia, respectively, with decent reproducibility among the biological replicates (R2 > 0.9, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation coefficients between biological replicates.

claim: The FLAG-tagged RpL3 in neurons was 7.8 times higher than in wild-type whole-head samples.
source: The FLAG-tagged RpL3 in the corresponding cells far exceeded the endogenous RpL3, as RpL3 reads were 7.8 and 42.7 times higher in neurons and glia, respectively, compared to the wild-type whole-head samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantified read counts comparing tagged to endogenous RpL3.

claim: The FLAG-tagged RpL3 in glia was 42.7 times higher than in wild-type whole-head samples.
source: The FLAG-tagged RpL3 in the corresponding cells far exceeded the endogenous RpL3, as RpL3 reads were 7.8 and 42.7 times higher in neurons and glia, respectively, compared to the wild-type whole-head samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantified read counts comparing tagged to endogenous RpL3.

claim: Known marker genes were strongly enriched while non-target markers were depleted in the cell-type-specific Ribo-seq.
source: The known marker genes were strongly enriched while non-target markers were depleted (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022), and the KEGG enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of footprints on genes associated with the known functions of these cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis results from their data and cites previous marker gene studies.

claim: KEGG enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of footprints on genes associated with the known functions of neurons and glial cells.
source: The known marker genes were strongly enriched while non-target markers were depleted (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C and D; Croset et al., 2018; Davie et al., 2018; Li et al., 2022), and the KEGG enrichment analysis showed significant enrichment of footprints on genes associated with the known functions of these cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports KEGG enrichment analysis results from their data.

claim: Neurons exhibit a greater extent of protein synthesis related to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial ribosome proteins.
source: Interestingly, the KEGG analysis also revealed that neurons exhibit a greater extent of protein synthesis related to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial ribosome proteins, while glial cells show higher expression of proteins associated with glycolysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports KEGG analysis results from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Glial cells show higher expression of proteins associated with glycolysis.
source: Interestingly, the KEGG analysis also revealed that neurons exhibit a greater extent of protein synthesis related to oxidative phosphorylation and mitochondrial ribosome proteins, while glial cells show higher expression of proteins associated with glycolysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports KEGG analysis results from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: The findings support the glia-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis.
source: These findings support the glia-neuron lactate shuttle hypothesis, a recently proposed concept of metabolic specialization (Mason, 2017; Volkenhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript interprets their findings in the context of a previously proposed hypothesis.

claim: Clustered ribosome footprints were detected on Hsr-ω, previously annotated as a long non-coding RNA.
source: Furthermore, apart from the annotated CDS, we detected clustered ribosome footprints on Hsr-ω, previously annotated as a long non-coding RNA, strongly suggesting the synthesis of hitherto undescribed polypeptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G; Singh, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome footprints on Hsr-ω from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: The ribosome footprints on Hsr-ω strongly suggest the synthesis of hitherto undescribed polypeptides.
source: Furthermore, apart from the annotated CDS, we detected clustered ribosome footprints on Hsr-ω, previously annotated as a long non-coding RNA, strongly suggesting the synthesis of hitherto undescribed polypeptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G; Singh, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript infers polypeptide synthesis from the presence of ribosome footprints.

claim: Genes mediating fatty acid metabolism and degradation showed lower TE in neurons or in glia compared to the whole head.
source: Genes mediating fatty acid metabolism and degradation, for example, were actively translated in the whole head, but showed lower TE in neurons or in glia (Figures 1H and 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative TE values from their data across different samples.

claim: Many fatty acid metabolism genes are highly expressed in the fat bodies.
source: Because many of these genes are highly expressed in the fat bodies (Dobson et al., 2018), these results suggest selective translational enhancement in the fat body.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing expression in fat bodies.

claim: The results suggest selective translational enhancement of fatty acid metabolism genes in the fat body.
source: Because many of these genes are highly expressed in the fat bodies (Dobson et al., 2018), these results suggest selective translational enhancement in the fat body.
evidence: The manuscript infers selective translational enhancement from their TE data and cited expression data.

claim: TE of genes involved in neuroactive ligand–receptor interaction was significantly higher in neurons but lower in glia.
source: Strikingly, TE of genes involved in neuroactive ligand–receptor interaction was significantly higher in neurons but lower in glia (Figure 2C and D), suggesting cell-type-specific translational regulation of these genes.
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative TE values from their data.

claim: The differential TE of neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction genes suggests cell-type-specific translational regulation.
source: Strikingly, TE of genes involved in neuroactive ligand–receptor interaction was significantly higher in neurons but lower in glia (Figure 2C and D), suggesting cell-type-specific translational regulation of these genes.
evidence: The manuscript infers cell-type-specific regulation from their TE data.

claim: There is a weak TE correlation between neurons and glia (R2 = 0.534).
source: This differential translational regulation was highlighted in the weak TE correlation between neurons and glia (R2 = 0.534, Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports a correlation coefficient calculated from their TE data.

claim: There is a genome-wide tendency that genes transcribed less in glia are further suppressed at translation.
source: We found a genome-wide tendency that genes transcribed less in glia are further suppressed at translation (Figure 2F).
evidence: The manuscript reports an observed trend from their genome-wide data analysis.

claim: Many functionally characterized neuronal genes showed particularly lower TE in glia.
source: Specifically, many functionally characterized neuronal genes, such as voltage- or ligand-gated ion channels, G-protein-coupled receptors, neuropeptides, and proteins for visual perception, showed particularly lower TE in glia (Figure 2E, G, and H. Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed TE values for these gene categories from their data.

claim: For neuronal genes, the distinction between neuronal and glial cells was much exaggerated at the level of translation than at transcription.
source: For these genes, the distinction between neuronal and glial cells was much exaggerated at the level of translation than at transcription (Figure 2H).
evidence: The manuscript compares the degree of distinction between RNA-seq and Ribo-seq data.

claim: The inter-cell-type correlation became weaker in Ribo-seq data compared to in RNA-seq (R2 = 0.59 vs. 0.81).
source: Consistently on the genome-wide scale, the inter-cell-type correlation became weaker in Ribo-seq data compared to in RNA-seq (R2 = 0.59 vs. 0.81, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation coefficients calculated from their data.

claim: Translational regulation contributes substantially to shaping cell-type-specific protein expression.
source: Altogether, these data indicate substantial contributions of translational regulation to shaping the cell-type-specific protein expression.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from their comparative transcriptome-translatome data.

claim: Fat-body-related genes showed lower TE in neurons compared to the whole head.
source: Fat-body-related genes showed lower TE in neurons compared to the whole head (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative TE values from their data.

claim: Among fat-body-related genes, there was a remarkable ribosomal accumulation on the start codon specifically in neurons.
source: Among these genes, we found a remarkable ribosomal accumulation on the start codon specifically in neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), as if the first round of the elongation cycle was arrested in neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome distribution patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: mRNAs showing strong ribosomal accumulation on the start codons are highly abundant in the fat bodies.
source: Through the reanalysis of the published RNA-seq data (Dobson et al., 2018), we found that mRNAs showing strong ribosomal accumulation on the start codons are highly abundant in the fat bodies (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings from reanalysis of published data.

claim: Glial ribosome footprints on DTTs suppressed in glia were remarkably biased toward 5′ leaders.
source: On the other hand, DTTs suppressed in glial cells compared to neurons (defined as genes with more than 10 times higher TE in neurons than in glia, n = 161), we noticed that glial ribosome footprints were remarkably biased toward 5′ leaders (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome distribution patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: The high 5′ leader/CDS ratio of ribosome footprints in glia was not obvious on the genome-wide scale.
source: Notably, this pattern was not obvious on the genome-wide scale (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of specific gene sets to genome-wide patterns.

claim: The high 5′ leader/CDS ratio of ribosome footprints in glia was commonly observed on many transcripts with known neuronal functions.
source: The high 5′ leader/CDS ratio of ribosome footprints in glia was commonly observed on many transcripts with known neuronal functions, such as Rab3, Syt4, Arr1, and Syn (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed patterns across multiple neuronal genes from their data.

claim: Accumulated ribosome footprints on the 5′ leaders of several glial marker genes were observed specifically in neurons.
source: Conversely, we observed accumulated ribosome footprints on the 5′ leaders of several glial marker genes specifically in neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome distribution patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Glial cells selectively suppress the protein synthesis of neuronal genes through uORF.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the translation of 5' leaders in selective mRNAs differentiates protein synthesis among cell types.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on their ribosome distribution data.

claim: Metagene plot around the AUG codons on 5′ leaders revealed strong accumulation of footprints on the upstream AUG codons.
source: Consistent with this idea, metagene plot around the AUG codons on 5′ leaders revealed strong accumulation of footprints on the upstream AUG codons, similar to those observed on the initiation codon of CDSs (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The manuscript reports metagene analysis results from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Upstream AUG and the near cognate codons (NUG or AUN) showed relatively high accumulation of footprints.
source: We calculated the footprint accumulation score on each codon (defined as the ratio of footprints on each codon with surrounding –50/+50 nt), and found that upstream AUG and the near cognate codons (NUG or AUN) showed relatively high accumulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated footprint accumulation scores from their data.

claim: Inside the annotated CDS, none of the codons exhibited significant accumulation.
source: On the other hand, inside the annotated CDS, none of the codons exhibited such significant accumulation (Figure 4D).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of footprint accumulation within CDS from their data.

claim: Transcripts related to neuronal functions typically contain long 5′ leaders and many upstream AUG.
source: Consistently, we found that transcripts related to neuronal functions typically contain long 5′ leaders and many upstream AUG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of 5′ leader characteristics from genome annotation.

claim: Glial cells suppress the translation of neuronal transcripts by stalling ribosomes on 5′ leader via uORF.
source: We thus propose that glial cells suppress the translation of neuronal transcripts by stalling ribosomes on 5′ leader via uORF.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism based on their ribosome distribution and uORF analysis.

claim: Active translation of Rh1 was almost exclusively observed in neurons.
source: We next asked whether the 5′ leader sequences of neuronal genes cause cell-type differences in translation. To this end, we focused on Rh1 (Rhodopsin 1, also known as ninaE), which encodes an opsin, also detecting stimuli of other sensory modalities (Leung et al., 2020; O'Tousa et al., 1985; Shen et al., 2011; Zuker et al., 1985). Consistently, active translation of Rh1 was almost exclusively observed in neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed translation levels from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Rh1 encodes an opsin that also detects stimuli of other sensory modalities.
source: We next asked whether the 5′ leader sequences of neuronal genes cause cell-type differences in translation. To this end, we focused on Rh1 (Rhodopsin 1, also known as ninaE), which encodes an opsin, also detecting stimuli of other sensory modalities (Leung et al., 2020; O'Tousa et al., 1985; Shen et al., 2011; Zuker et al., 1985).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies characterizing Rh1 function.

claim: The distribution of ribosome footprints on Rh1 was distinct among neuronal and glial cells, with footprints heavily biased to 5′ leader in glia.
source: Similar to other neuronal genes shown in Figure 3C, the distribution of ribosome footprints was distinct among neuronal and glial cells: they were heavily biased to 5′ leader in glia, with the striking accumulation on the putative uORFs composed only of the start and stop codons (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome distribution patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: There was striking accumulation of ribosome footprints on the putative uORFs of Rh1 composed only of the start and stop codons in glia.
source: Similar to other neuronal genes shown in Figure 3C, the distribution of ribosome footprints was distinct among neuronal and glial cells: they were heavily biased to 5′ leader in glia, with the striking accumulation on the putative uORFs composed only of the start and stop codons (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome accumulation patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: The Rh1 reporter mRNA was detected both in neuronal and glial cells when driven by Tub-GAL4.
source: To address the function of these sequences on differential translation, we constructed a transgenic reporter strain using the Rh1 UTR sequences under the control of UAS (Figure 5D), and directed gene expression ubiquitously using Tub-GAL4. While the reporter mRNA was detected both in neuronal and glial cells, the protein levels were much more heterogeneous and strikingly weak in glia (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed mRNA distribution from fluorescent in situ hybridization.

claim: The Rh1 reporter protein levels were much more heterogeneous and strikingly weak in glia when driven by Tub-GAL4.
source: To address the function of these sequences on differential translation, we constructed a transgenic reporter strain using the Rh1 UTR sequences under the control of UAS (Figure 5D), and directed gene expression ubiquitously using Tub-GAL4. While the reporter mRNA was detected both in neuronal and glial cells, the protein levels were much more heterogeneous and strikingly weak in glia (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed protein distribution from fluorescence imaging.

claim: The control reporter strain exhibited more ubiquitous expression, with significantly higher fluorescent intensity in glia.
source: The control reporter strain (DeLuca and Spradling, 2018), on the other hand, exhibited more ubiquitous expression, with significantly higher fluorescent intensity in glia (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed protein distribution from fluorescence imaging and cites the control strain source.

claim: When the six-base putative uORFs were mutated, the in vivo protein-to-mRNA ratio of the reporter was significantly increased in glia but not in neurons.
source: Strikingly, when the six-base putative uORFs were mutated, the in vivo protein-to-mRNA ratio of the reporter was significantly increased in glia but not in neurons (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantified protein-to-mRNA ratios from imaging data comparing wild-type and mutant reporters.

claim: The small upstream open-reading frames in the 5' leader confer selective translational suppression in glia.
source: Using transgenic reporter strains, we provide evidence that the small upstream open-reading frames in the 5' leader confer selective translational suppression in glia.
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental evidence from transgenic reporter experiments.

claim: Translational efficiency of proteins fundamental to neuronal functions, such as ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors, was maintained low in glia, leading to their preferential translation in neurons.
source: Specifically, we found that translational efficiency of proteins fundamental to neuronal functions, such as ion channels and neurotransmitter receptors, was maintained low in glia, leading to their preferential translation in neurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports calculated TE values from their comparative Ribo-seq data.

claim: Distribution of ribosome footprints on neuronal mRNAs exhibited a remarkable bias toward the 5′ leaders in glia.
source: Notably, distribution of ribosome footprints on these mRNAs exhibited a remarkable bias toward the 5′ leaders in glia.
evidence: The manuscript reports observed ribosome distribution patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Translational regulation enhances distinction of cell types in the nervous system.
source: Translational regulation enhances distinction of cell types in the nervous system
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the manuscript, supported by their comparative transcriptome-translatome data.

claim: The characteristic feature of long 5′ leaders containing numerous uORFs is also observed in neuronal transcripts in mammals.
source: This characteristic feature of long 5′ leaders containing numerous uORFs is also observed in neuronal transcripts in mammals (Glock et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing similar features in mammalian neuronal transcripts.

claim: 5′ leader-mediated translational regulations are known to be critical for quick response to environmental changes, such as starvation or oxidative stress.
source: While the 5′ leader-mediated translational regulations are known to be critical for quick response to environmental changes, such as starvation or oxidative stress (Harding et al., 2003; Mueller and Hinnebusch, 1986; Young and Wek, 2016), our study sheds light on its roles in contrasting protein expression among cell types.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on 5′ leader-mediated regulation.

claim: De novo protein synthesis plays a pivotal role for long-lasting adaptation.
source: Furthermore, considering a pivotal role of de novo protein synthesis for long-lasting adaptation (Flexner et al., 1963; Tully et al., 1994), it is plausible that similar mechanisms are employed for neuronal plasticity as well.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on protein synthesis and adaptation.

claim: Similar mechanisms to those described in the study may be employed for neuronal plasticity.
source: Furthermore, considering a pivotal role of de novo protein synthesis for long-lasting adaptation (Flexner et al., 1963; Tully et al., 1994), it is plausible that similar mechanisms are employed for neuronal plasticity as well.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential roles based on cited literature.

claim: eIF1, eIF2α kinases, and DENR/MCT1 are facilitators of translation of main ORF whose 5′ leaders harbor uORFs.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have identified eIF1, eIF2α kinases, and DENR/MCT1 as facilitators of translation of main ORF whose 5′ leaders harbor uORFs (Ivanov et al., 2010; Schleich et al., 2014; Sonenberg and Hinnebusch, 2009; Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies identifying these factors.

claim: eIF1, eIF2α kinases, and DENR/MCT1 are expressed more in neurons than in glia.
source: Interestingly, all these proteins are expressed more in neurons than in glia in our dataset (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression levels from their RNA-seq data.

claim: Selective activation of eIF1, eIF2α kinases, and DENR/MCT1 might underlie the cell-type-specific translation.
source: Selective activation of these molecular machineries might underlie the cell-type-specific translation.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about potential mechanisms based on their expression data.

claim: Transition from initiation to elongation may serve as another regulatory checkpoint of protein synthesis.
source: Therefore, transition from initiation to elongation may serve as another regulatory checkpoint of protein synthesis (Harnett et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019), which enhances cell-type distinctions.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from their ribosome stalling data and cites related studies.

claim: Stop-codon readthrough has been reported to be more frequent in neurons than in other cell types.
source: Stop-codon readthrough has been reported to be more frequent in neurons than in other cell types (Hudson et al., 2021; Karki et al., 2022; Prieto-Godino et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on stop-codon readthrough.

claim: Readthrough events extend the protein C-terminus.
source: Because the readthrough events extend the protein C-terminus, its regulation can add yet another layer of cell-type diversity (Dunn et al., 2013; Jungreis et al., 2011; Klagges et al., 1996).
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge and cites supporting studies.

claim: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation, while glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports ribosome allocation patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: Glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates.
source: Neurons allocate more ribosomes to proteins related to neurotransmission, visual sensing, and oxidative phosphorylation, while glial cells synthesize transporters and enzymes for metabolism of amino acid, fatty acid, or carbohydrates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript reports protein synthesis patterns from their Ribo-seq data.

claim: A significant amount of neuronal and glial cells has a common developmental origin from neuro-glioblasts.
source: Despite these clear differences and specialization, a significant amount of neuronal and glial cells has a common developmental origin. They originate from a stem cell lineage known as neuro-glioblasts (Lai and Lee, 2006; Viktorin et al., 2011), and the fate of these cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm) (Hartenstein, 2011; Hosoya et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on developmental origins.

claim: The fate of neuro-glioblast cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm).
source: They originate from a stem cell lineage known as neuro-glioblasts (Lai and Lee, 2006; Viktorin et al., 2011), and the fate of these cells can be altered by the expression of a single gene, glial cells missing (gcm) (Hartenstein, 2011; Hosoya et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on cell fate determination.

claim: Translational regulations may play a particularly important role in neuronal and glial sister cell types with distinct physiological roles.
source: Therefore, translational regulations, in addition to transcriptional diversity, may play a particularly important role in these sister cell types with distinct physiological roles.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from their data on translational regulation and cited developmental biology.

claim: In the Drosophila brain, approximately 100 stem cell lineages diverge into more than 5000 morphologically distinct cell types.
source: In the Drosophila brain, approximately 100 stem cell lineages diverge into more than 5000 morphologically distinct cell types (Ito et al., 2013; Scheffer et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies on Drosophila brain cell diversity.

claim: Translational regulations may play significant roles in differentiating neuronal or glial subtypes.
source: Hence, translational regulations similar to those described in this study, or other possible regulations, may play significant roles in further differentiating neuronal or glial subtypes.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about broader implications of their findings.

claim: The UAS-Rh1-Venus reporter showed heterogeneous expression even among neurons.
source: Consistent with this idea, our UAS-Rh1-Venus reporter showed heterogeneous expression even among neurons, contrasting with the more uniform expression observed in the control UASz-GFP reporter (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript reports observed expression patterns from imaging data.

claim: ChAT and VAChT are transcribed in many glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons but their protein synthesis is inhibited.
source: In accordance, choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), an enzyme needed to synthesize acetylcholine, and vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) are transcribed in many glutamatergic and GABAergic neurons but its protein synthesis is inhibited (Chen et al., 2023; Lacin et al., 2019).
